name: Question 2
problem:
Consider the d’Alembert differential equation

$$
y=x(3+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})+2{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}.
$$

If ${y}^{′}(x)=t,$ then general solution can be expressed in parametric form $(x(t),y(t)),$ where

$$
x(t)=C{e}^{-t/3}+f(t)
$$

and $C$ is an arbitrary constant. Find the function $f(t).$

*Hint: Under the given transformation, we have*

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{3}x=-\frac{4}{3}t.
$$

*You may also wish to make use of the following result (constants omitted):*

$$
\int t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t=(t-1){e}^{t}
$$
worked_solution:
A differential equation is a d'Alembert differential equation if it can be expressed in the form

$$
y=xf({y}^{′})+g({y}^{′}),
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are differentiable functions of ${y}^{′}.$ 

We're told that, under the substitution ${y}^{′}(x)=t,$ our d’Alembert differential equation transforms to the first-order linear equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{3}x=-\frac{4}{3}t.
$$

We'll solve this equation using the method of integrating factors. Since this equation is already of the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+P(t)x=Q(t),
$$

we compute our integrating factor as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int P(t)\,\text{d}t}={e}^{\int \frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}t}={e}^{t/3}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying our differential equation by $I(t)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{t/3}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{3}x{e}^{t/3} & =-\frac{4}{3}t{e}^{t/3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Rewriting the left-hand side as an exact derivative, and integrating both sides of the equation with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x{e}^{t/3}) & =-\frac{4}{3}t{e}^{t/3} \\ \int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x{e}^{t/3})\,\text{d}t & =-\frac{4}{3}\int t{e}^{t/3}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

To evaluate the integral, let $u=\frac{t}{3}.$ Then $t=3u$ and $\text{d}t=3\,\text{d}u,$ so

$$
\begin{aligned}\int t{e}^{t/3}\,\text{d}t & =\int (3u){e}^{u}\cdot 3\,\text{d}u \\  & =9\int u{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =9(u-1){e}^{u}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting back $u=\frac{t}{3},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int t{e}^{t/3}\,\text{d}t & =9(\frac{t}{3}-1){e}^{t/3} \\  & =(3t-9){e}^{t/3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}x{e}^{t/3} & =-\frac{4}{3}(3t-9){e}^{t/3}+C \\  & =(-4t+12){e}^{t/3}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

which gives

$$
x=-4t+12+C{e}^{-t/3}.
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
x(t)=C{e}^{-t/3}+12-4t
$$

and finally, $f(t)=12-4t.$

Consider the d’Alembert differential equation

y=x(3+dydx)+2(dydx)2.

If y′(x)=t, then general solution can be expressed in parametric form (x(t),y(t)), where

x(t)=Ce−t/3+f(t) and C is an arbitrary constant. Find the function f(t).

Hint: Under the given transformation, we have dxdt+13x=−43t. You may also wish to make use of the following result (constants omitted): ∫tetdt=(t−1)et

a
f(t)=12+4t
b
f(t)=9−4t
c
f(t)=12−2t
d
f(t)=12−4t
e
f(t)=4−12t

EXPLANATION

A differential equation is a d'Alembert differential equation if it can be expressed in the form

y=xf(y′)+g(y′), where f and g are differentiable functions of y′.

We're told that, under the substitution y′(x)=t, our d’Alembert differential equation transforms to the first-order linear equation

dxdt+13x=−43t.

We'll solve this equation using the method of integrating factors. Since this equation is already of the form

dxdt+P(t)x=Q(t), we compute our integrating factor as follows: I(t)=e∫P(t)dt=e∫13dt=et/3

Multiplying our differential equation by I(t) gives et/3dxdt+13xet/3=−43tet/3.

Rewriting the left-hand side as an exact derivative, and integrating both sides of the equation with respect to t, we have ddt(xet/3)=−43tet/3∫ddt(xet/3)dt=−43∫tet/3dt.

To evaluate the integral, let u=t3. Then t=3u and dt=3du, so ∫tet/3dt=∫(3u)eu⋅3du=9∫ueudu=9(u−1)eu.

Substituting back u=t3, we get ∫tet/3dt=9(t3−1)et/3=(3t−9)et/3.

Therefore, xet/3=−43(3t−9)et/3+C=(−4t+12)et/3+C, which gives x=−4t+12+Ce−t/3.

Therefore, we have that x(t)=Ce−t/3+12−4t and finally, f(t)=12−4t.
